drafts.headline: Cost of sales forecasts run about 1.8 times too low for AMOC.
drafts.plain: The method misses this driver in the same direction almost every time, not at random. That is a fixable defect rather than noise — find what is wired wrong before adding any correction factor.
drafts.evidence: Bias -0.579 log (about 1.8 times too low), average miss 0.579, wrong in the same direction in 100% of cases, and the sign holds across every bootstrap block tested (n=9).
drafts.why_scope: A robust bias in one driver may be this company's disclosure, its whole class's economics, or our method. Decide which before filing.
drafts.overturned_by: A later run of the same name where the sign no longer holds across bootstrap blocks.
drafts.declined: The same defect counted again. This driver's bias is one consequence of the single specification error registered from DRAFT-AMOC-08 — an inconsistent macro scenario drags every nominal line the same way at once. Thirteen entries for one cause would bury the finding rather than record it.

drafts.headline: A forecast scenario must be internally consistent, or it invents its own bias.
drafts.plain: If you carry inflation forward at 25% a year, you cannot also hold the exchange rate still — those are the same event seen twice. Doing both inflates every cost and freezes every price, and the profit forecast is then wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with the company. Check that the macro assumptions could all be true at once before reading anything into the errors they produce.
drafts.evidence: Bias -0.570 log (about 1.8 times too low), average miss 0.570, wrong in the same direction in 100% of cases, and the sign holds across every bootstrap block tested (n=9).
drafts.why_scope: This is a rule about how a scenario is built, not about refining or about Egypt. Any model that escalates costs on one index and revenue on another can do it.
drafts.overturned_by: A scenario whose macro inputs are mutually inconsistent that nonetheless produces no directional bias in the lines they drive.

drafts.headline: The gross profit forecast loses to assuming no change.
drafts.plain: At 3 of 3 horizons, simply carrying last year's number forward beat the model. A method that cannot beat 'no change' has not earned the precision it displays, and should be published as a range or not at all.
drafts.evidence: Negative skill against the freeze benchmark at horizons 1, 2, 3, worst -0.835.
drafts.why_scope: Losing to a naive benchmark usually points at the method, which would make it ALL — but confirm it is not this company's series being unusually persistent.
drafts.overturned_by: A later run where the model beats the freeze benchmark at a majority of horizons.
drafts.declined: The same finding counted again. The profit stack is one number arrived at through several subtotals, and it losing to no-change is registered once from DRAFT-AMOC-16.

drafts.headline: Test the method against 'assume no change' before trusting its profit forecast.
drafts.plain: The simplest possible forecast is to write down last year's number and stop. It is surprisingly hard to beat, and a model that loses to it has not earned the precision it displays. Run the comparison explicitly — if the model loses, publish a range and say so, rather than a point that looks more informed than it is.
drafts.evidence: Negative skill against the freeze benchmark at horizons 1, 2, 3, worst -1.588.
drafts.why_scope: A method rule about how any forecast is validated. Nothing in it is about refining, about Egypt, or about this company.
drafts.overturned_by: A run where the model beats the no-change benchmark on the profit line at every horizon tested.

drafts.headline: Setting 'non-recurring' items to zero is a forecast, and usually a bad one.
drafts.plain: Provision releases, disposal gains and currency gains are each unpredictable, so the tempting rule is to forecast none of them. But something in that bucket lands almost every year, and zero is further from the truth than simply carrying last year's total forward. If the individual items cannot be forecast, forecast the bucket.
drafts.evidence: Negative skill against the freeze benchmark at horizons 1, 2, 3, worst -0.785.
drafts.why_scope: A rule about how a residual income line is treated, and every issuer has one. The specific items differ; the error of zeroing them does not.
drafts.overturned_by: An issuer whose other-income line is genuinely empty in most years, where zero beats carrying the previous year forward.

drafts.headline: A number that is zero by construction is not a finding about the world.
drafts.plain: If a driver contains no inflation term, then re-running it with perfect knowledge of inflation must change nothing, and the 'macro share' of its error must come back at exactly zero. That is arithmetic, not evidence. Declare which drivers those are BEFORE running the split, so a structural zero cannot be read back as a discovery.
drafts.evidence: Average miss 0.606 as known, 0.606 with perfect foresight of inflation — the macro share is only 0.0%.
drafts.why_scope: A rule about reading a decomposition, and it applies wherever an error is split into parts. It was earned here by an automated draft that offered three structural zeros as though they were results.
drafts.overturned_by: Nothing. A quantity fixed by construction cannot become evidence about the world.

drafts.headline: On a thin spread, being right about both sides separately is not enough.
drafts.plain: When profit is a small difference between two very large numbers, an error that looks tiny on each of them is enormous on the difference. Six per cent out on revenue and almost exact on cost still left the gross profit forecast wrong by two thirds. What has to be right is the two sides RELATIVE to each other, and a model that forecasts them independently will not deliver that however good each looks alone.
drafts.evidence: Average miss 0.504 as known, 0.519 with perfect foresight of inflation — the macro share is only -2.8%.
drafts.why_scope: Filed to the spread class rather than to every study, because the mechanism needs a thin residual between two large flows. A business earning a 40% margin can absorb the same relative errors without the profit line moving much. It is filed at the narrower scope and will widen if a second spread business shows the same thing.
drafts.overturned_by: A pass-through business with a comparably thin margin where independent revenue and cost forecasts of similar accuracy produce a proportionate, not amplified, profit error.
drafts.applies_to: refiner, commodity pass-through on a thin spread

drafts.headline: The investment revenues error is the company, not the currency.
drafts.plain: Re-running every forecast with perfect foresight of inflation barely improves it. So devaluation is not the explanation, and looking for a macro fix would waste the effort.
drafts.evidence: Average miss 1.453 as known, 1.453 with perfect foresight of inflation — the macro share is only 0.0%.
drafts.why_scope: Almost always ALL — 'check whether the macro explains it before assuming it does' is a method rule — but the specific finding may be about this market.
drafts.overturned_by: A market or period where the same decomposition puts most of the error on the macro path.
drafts.declined: A structural zero, not a measurement: this driver is a level-persistence rule with no inflation and no crude term, declared as such in the pre-registration, so its macro share must be zero by construction. The lesson that this is not a finding is registered once from DRAFT-AMOC-21.

drafts.headline: The claims provision bias changes direction between regimes.
drafts.plain: It runs one way in one period and the other way in the next. Averaging them produces a correction that is wrong in both. Record it, do not correct for it.
drafts.evidence: By era: E1 pre-devaluation -0.954; E2 devaluation +0.421.
drafts.why_scope: A sign that flips with the regime is usually about the market or the period, not the company — but say which.
drafts.overturned_by: A longer record in which one sign dominates across all regimes.
drafts.declined: Degenerate era test. The pre-devaluation era holds ONE origin in this window, so a 'sign change between regimes' here is a comparison of three cells against six on a driver that is held flat by rule. The pre-registration said in advance that the era split could not be load-bearing at five origins.

drafts.headline: Check an annualised half-year base against every full year you hold.
drafts.plain: A base year built by doubling one good half can sit well above anything the company has actually achieved over twelve months. Growing from it then compounds a rebound into a trend. Before forecasting growth off a part-year base, line it up against the full-year record — and if the base is already the highest number in that record, flat is the optimistic case, not the neutral one.
drafts.evidence: AMOC's base half annualises to 1,616,167 tonnes against a five-year mean of 1,436,781 and a most recent full year of 1,261,586; audited sales tonnage ran 1,492,273 / 1,547,816 / 1,448,889 / 1,433,341 / 1,261,586 over FY2021-FY2025. Even a FLAT volume rule over-forecast, bias +7.6% and too high in 8 of 9 tested cases.
drafts.why_scope: A rule about constructing a base year, not about refining. It is recorded by judgement rather than by the automated draft: the volume bias is 0.073 log, below the 0.20 threshold fixed in the harvester before any run, so the selection rule did not raise it. The threshold was NOT changed to capture it — that would be tuning after seeing the numbers. The evidence above is the run's own measured figures.
drafts.overturned_by: A part-year base that is representative of the full-year record, where growing from it does not over-forecast.
